asymbiotic mycelium, exploring the rhizosphere with a typically negative geotropism. The perception of
root exudates triggers presymbiotic hyphal branching, culminating in the formation of a hyphopodium on

Figure 8.1 Stages of mycorrhization and signaling events involved. Plant roots release strigolactones,
which induce arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) spore germination and branching. The transcription factors
NSP1 (Nodulation Signaling Pathway 1) and NSP2 are required for strigolactone production. In turn, AM
fungi release signaling molecules called Myc factors. These are recognized at the plasma membrane by as
yet unidentified Myc factor receptors that act together with SYMRK (SYMbiosis Receptor‐like Kinase).
Putative secondary messengers transduce the signal to the nucleus to activate perinuclear calcium spiking.
Proteins involved in the generation of calcium spiking are CASTOR and POLLUX, the calcium ATPase
MCA8, NUP85 (NUCLEOPORIN85), NUP133, the nucleoporin NENA, and a putative calcium channel.
The calcium response is decoded by CCaMK (Calcium‐ and calmodulin‐dependent protein kinase), which
phosphorylates and, thereby, activates the transcription factor CYCLOPS. RAM1 (Required for Arbuscular
Mycorrhization 1) is required at the stage of hyphopodium formation at the root epidermis. CYCLOPS is
important during the spreading of intraradical hyphae in the cortex. RAM1, RAD1 (Required for
Arbuscule Development), DIP1 (Della Interacting Protein 1), DELLAs and CYCLOPS are required for
arbuscule development in the inner cortex of the root. (See insert for color representation of the figure.)

Figure 16.1 Cellular mechanisms of trace element homeostasis and detoxification in ECM fungi. Uptake
from the soil depends on different factors: (1a) Trace elements may be immobilized in the soil by
extracellular ligands or by binding to the cell wall. (1b) Transport across the plasma membrane is regulated
by different in‐ and efflux transporters. (1c) Net uptake may also depend on the secretory pathway. (2)
Once in the cytosol, trace elements are efficiently sequestered by different types of ligands. (3a) Excess
elements may be stored in the vacuole and remobilized in periods of deficiency. (3b) Alternatively, excess
Zn may be transported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and stored in ER related vesicles or
zincosomes. TE – trace element; CTR – copper transporter; CDF – cation diffusion facilitator; ABC – ATP
binding cassette; ZIP – Zrt/Irt‐like protein; cys – cysteine; GSH – glutathione; PC – phytochelatin;
MT – metallothionein. (See insert for color representation of the figure.)

Figure 19.1 Regional differentiation of ectomycorrhizal fungal communities. The non‐metric
multidimensional scaling (NMDS) ordination shows community similarity of ectomycorrhizal fungi
detected in 561 individual soils cores through second generation DNA sequencing of the ITS region.
Soil cores were collected from essentially monodominant natural Pine stands soils across North America.
Geographic location (color) and soil horizon (symbol) are mapped onto soil cores according to the legend.
Ectomycorrhizal fungi communities cluster primarily by geographic locality from which they were sampled.
There was little effect of soil horizon on community similarity at the continental scale, despite strong,
consistent changes in soil chemistry across organic (OH) and mineral (AH) horizons. These results
demonstrate that biogeographic factors are the first order determinants of ectomycorrhizal community
structure. (See insert for color representation of the figure.)

Figure 19.2 The use of molecular phylogenies to infer past events shaping current day distribution patterns
in ectomycorrhizal fungi. The phylogeny depicts three different scenarios to explain the modern‐day
disjunction between species found in the grey and white areas, as indicated by colored symbols at the tips
of the phylogeny. Gaps between areas indicate large barriers (oceans, mountains) across which species
cannot easily move. Different scenarios depend primarily on the timing of connections between the grey
and white areas at the node marked with a*. In scenario (a), the split between grey and white taxa is
driven by a vicariant event that breaks up the ancestral range, followed by speciation. In scenario
(b), the separation of the two areas predates the origin of the white lineage, and so must result from
dispersal (arrow) across the barrier, followed by speciation. In scenario (c), the origin of the white lineages
corresponds with the occurrence of a temporary land bridge, suggesting overland migration followed by
speciation.

Figure 21.1 (after Read and Perez‐Moreno, 2003) In a latitudinal/altitudinal gradient from grassland, via
deciduous and coniferous forest to heathland, nitrogen availability and soil mixing increase towards
deciduous forests and grasslands. Conversely, environmental stress and the relative allocation of carbon
to roots increase towards coniferous forests and heaths. Viewed as C‐strategists, ectomycorrhizal fungi,
together with other Agaricomycetes are, in general, favored by high carbon and nitrogen availability,
but disfavored by environmental stress and mixing disturbance. Thus, the romboidal area in the
centre represents the ectomycorrhizal niche. The gradient is maintained by positive feedback
mechanisms:(1) Towards heaths, environmental stress in terms of low nitrogen availability, acidic soils,
cold temperatures and dry soils favors S‐strategists (such as many Leotiomycetes and members of the
Chaetothyriales). These fungi frequently have melanized cell‐walls, with low turnover of both biomass
and necromass, and reduced enzymatic capacity compared with basidiomycetes. These features, in turn,
lead to organic matter accumulation and further intensified N limitation. (2) Towards grasslands, low
and/or irregular carbon availability, as well as a high level of disturbance by soil fauna, favors R‐
strategists (bacteria, Zygomycetes and many members of the Hypocreales). Here, rapid turnover of
organic matter feeds back on high availability of inorganic nitrogen. In the absence of external nitrogen
inputs and intense forest management, ectomycorrhizal fungal abundance correlates positively with
soil fertility within boreal forests (Clemmensen et al., 2015; Sterkenburg et al., 2015). This suggests that
the maximum ectomycorrhizal abundance coincides roughly with the transition from coniferous to
deciduous forest. However, disturbances such as fertilization, clearcutting or nitrogen deposition, which
interfere with ecosystem feedbacks, may push boreal forests past this transition, reducing
ectomycorrhizal abundance.

Figure 26.1 Summary of biomass and some of the key interactions of mycorrhizal fungi in the soil
ecosystem in typical arbuscular mycorrhizal ecosystems based on temperate and tropical grasslands and for
ectomycorrhizal ecosystems based on boreal and coniferous forest (data adapted from Petersen and
Luxton, 1982; Fogel and Hunt, 1983; Jackson et al., 1997; Högberg and Högberg, 2002; Treseder and Cross,
2006; Clemmensen et al., 2013), using an assumed depth of 0.1 m and bulk density of 1000 kg m–3 for
conversions where necessary; numbers should be viewed as indications of order‐of‐magnitude size of
pools). Grey shading indicates biomass or pool sizes that are generally higher under forest than grassland,
but see Dickie et al. (2014). Essentially, all boxes interact with all other boxes through predation,
competition, nutrient uptake, release and mortality; a subset of these resource flows are shown as thin
arrows. Some connections of interest, indicated by thicker arrows and numbers in circles, include: (1)
priming of saprotrophic decomposition by root and mycorrhizal exudation of C and N (Drake et al., 2013;
Finzi et al., 2015; Hodge and Storer, 2015), which can accelerate decomposition, and (2) results in trophic
cascade of increasing bacterial feeding nematodes and protozoans and their predators (Wardle, 2002).
Conversely, (3) organic nutrient use by ectomycorrhizal fungi removing N and P but not C, can result in
inhibition of nutrient mineralization by saprotrophs (Orwin et al., 2011) and may drive exclusion of
saprotrophic fungi from deeper soil layers in some systems (Lindahl et al., 2007). Preferential grazing by soil
fauna on saprotrophic fungi (4) may reduce competition with mycorrhizal fungi. Both saprotrophic and
ectomycorrhizal fungi may also kill and consume nematodes and collembola (5) as a source of N
(Klironomos and Hart, 2001).

Figure 7.3 Model for Nod factor and Myc‐LCO signaling pathways leading to nodulation, mycorrhization and
lateral root formation in Medicago truncatula. Key plant genes are indicated: NFP and LYK3 control signal
perception; DMI1, DMI2, DMI3 and NSP2 code for components of the Common Symbiosis Signaling Pathway
(CSSP), and Ram1 and NSP1 are predicted to control symbiotic signaling downstream of the CSSP, although
NSP1 intervenes in both Nod and Myc signaling, and both NSP1‐dependent and NSP1‐independent
Myc‐LCO-induced differential gene expression has been observed (see text). CSSP‐independent Myc‐LCO
signaling is proposed, based on transcriptomic studies (see text).

Figure 8.1 Stages of mycorrhization and signaling events involved. Plant roots release strigolactones, which
induce arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) spore germination and branching. The transcription factors NSP1
(Nodulation Signaling Pathway 1) and NSP2 are required for strigolactone production. In turn, AM fungi
release signaling molecules called Myc factors. These are recognized at the plasma membrane by as yet
unidentified Myc factor receptors that act together with SYMRK (SYMbiosis Receptor‐like Kinase). Putative
secondary messengers transduce the signal to the nucleus to activate perinuclear calcium spiking. Proteins
involved in the generation of calcium spiking are CASTOR and POLLUX, the calcium ATPase MCA8, NUP85
(NUCLEOPORIN85), NUP133, the nucleoporin NENA, and a putative calcium channel. The calcium
response is decoded by CCaMK (Calcium‐ and calmodulin‐dependent protein kinase), which
phosphorylates and, thereby, activates the transcription factor CYCLOPS. RAM1 (Required for Arbuscular
Mycorrhization 1) is required at the stage of hyphopodium formation at the root epidermis. CYCLOPS is
important during the spreading of intraradical hyphae in the cortex. RAM1, RAD1 (Required for Arbuscule
Development), DIP1 (Della Interacting Protein 1), DELLAs and CYCLOPS are required for arbuscule
development in the inner cortex of the root.

Figure 16.1 Cellular mechanisms of trace element homeostasis and detoxification in ECM fungi. Uptake
from the soil depends on different factors: (1a) Trace elements may be immobilized in the soil by
extracellular ligands or by binding to the cell wall. (1b) Transport across the plasma membrane is regulated
by different in‐ and efflux transporters. (1c) Net uptake may also depend on the secretory pathway.
(2) Once in the cytosol, trace elements are efficiently sequestered by different types of ligands. (3a) Excess
elements may be stored in the vacuole and remobilized in periods of deficiency. (3b) Alternatively, excess
Zn may be transported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and stored in ER related vesicles or
zincosomes. TE – trace element; CTR – copper transporter; CDF – cation diffusion facilitator; ABC – ATP
binding cassette; ZIP – Zrt/Irt‐like protein; cys – cysteine; GSH – glutathione; PC – phytochelatin;
MT – metallothionein.

Figure 16.3 Trace element detoxification in AM and ERM fungal‐plant associations. Non‐essential and excess
elements can be excluded from extra‐radical mycelium (E) to reduce their transfer to the intra‐radical mycelium
(I) and the host plant. Excess elements entering the extra‐radical mycelium will induce anti‐oxidative and repair
mechanisms. They will accumulate preferably in extra‐radical mycelium and spores (S). Excess elements
reaching intra‐radical mycelium can be accumulated in arbuscules (A) or be bound to pectin in the interfacial
matrix (im) around hyphal coils (HC) to reduce transfer to the plant. TE, trace element; direction of active
transport; inhibited/reduced transport; induction of antioxidative and repair mechanisms; c, conidia; cp,
conidiophores; Ep, epidermal cells; CC, cortical cells; En, endodermis; VC, vascular cylinder.

Figure 19.1 Regional differentiation of ectomycorrhizal fungal communities. The non-metric multidimensional
scaling (NMDS) ordination shows community similarity of ectomycorrhizal fungi detected in 561 individual
soils cores through second generation DNA sequencing of the ITS region. Soil cores were collected from
essentially monodominant natural Pine stands soils across North America. Geographic location and soil horizon
are both mapped onto soil cores according to the keys. Ectomycorrhizal fungi communities cluster primarily by
geographic locality from which they were sampled. There was little effect of soil horizon on community
similarity at the continental scale, despite strong, consistent changes in soil chemistry across organic (OH) and
mineral (AH) horizons. These results demonstrate that biogeographic factors are the first order determinants of
ectomycorrhizal community structure.

Figure 25.1 Nutrition of mycohetero‐ and mixotrophic plants associated with ectomycorrhizal fungi that
themselves associate with surrounding trees. In this model representing the usual situation in temperate
ecosystems, N flow from soil (blue) and C flow from photosynthesis (orange) are displayed, and the red
line indicates the interface between autotrophic host tree and ectomycorrhizal fungi where isotopic
fractionation occurs (enrichment in 13C from host to fungus and depletion in 15N from fungus to host).
